17-18 February, 2027 | Leeds, UK

Conference Theme: Challenges to Monetary Policy

The Department of Economics at the University of Leeds, in partnership with the Bank of England, is organising an in-person joint workshop on "Challenges to Monetary Policy". The event will take place in person in Leeds, UK, on 17th–18th February 2027.

The workshop features a confirmed keynote speech fromHuw Pill(Chief Economist, Bank of England). The organizers are inviting research addressing contemporary and future challenges across core themes:

  • Central bank autonomy: Navigating modern systemic risks.
  • Central bank communication: Strategies and public efficacy.
  • CBDCs: Global development and macro challenges.
  • Dual-pillar frameworks: Design and operational insights.
  • Inflation targeting: The structural future and historical lessons.
  • Geopolitical risks: Implications for absolute price stability.
  • Inflation dynamics: Assessing multi-order core shocks.
  • Policy transmission: Dynamics in hyper-dynamic environments.
  • Labor markets: Intersections with monetary frameworks.
  • Trade disruptions: Supply shocks and trade wars.
  • Biophysical neutrality: Ecological limits of central banking.
  • Fiscal interactions: Ensuring fiscal and monetary stability.
  • Regional disparities: Distributional impacts of policies.
  • Global spillovers: International spillovers and spillbacks.

The organizers would be deeply grateful if you could also share this call for papers with colleagues or any networks you think might be interested in submitting.

Please email your paper or abstract directly to Muhammad Ali Nasir.

Key Workshop Details:

  • Submission Deadline: 10th December 2026
  • Acceptance Notification: 20th December 2026
  • Logistics: There is no attendance fee. The event is in-person only, and participants are responsible for arranging and funding their own travel and accommodation.

Submission Deadline: 10 December, 2026

[Call for Papers] Call for Proposals for Special Issues in the Socio-Economic Review https://www.heterodoxnews.com/n/htn363.html#art-17592186132099 https://www.heterodoxnews.com/n/htn363.html#art-17592186132099#363 Call for Papers Mon, 24 Aug 2026 00:00:00 +0000

Deadline: 30 September 2026

Socio-Economic Review (SER) is pleased to invite proposals for Special Issues to be published in 2027 or 2028.

A Special Issue is a peer reviewed collection of articles on a specific theme. The theme should normally focus on a new or distinctive area of inquiry insufficiently explored in socio-economic literature, has a broad relevance, and falls within the aims and scope of the journal. Thereby, a special issue provides an opportunity to collectively explore a new topic, develop insightful new lines of research and exchange in dialogue across disciplines such as sociology, political science, economics, business, law, or history.

The proposal should contain the following information:

  1. The names, contact details, and positions of the proposed Guest Editors together with brief biographical details.
  2. The title of the proposed special issue.
  3. A one-page Call for Papers indicating the main theme, key topics, and methodological foci for submissions to the Special Issue.
  4. A list containing titles and short abstracts of any potential contributions, information about the authors and indication of their commitment. Guest editors are not permitted to submit regular peer review papers for the special issue but are encouraged to write a substantive introductory article developing the state of the art around the topic.
  5. A description of the behind the proposal, its planned scope, innovative nature in relation to existing published work, and likely relevance for readers of Socio-Economic Review. Please read the Editorial Policy Statement of SER via the following webpage:
  6. An envisioned timetable including a deadline for the first submission, a period for review and resubmission, and deadline for final print-ready papers.

The team of Guest Editors for the Special Issue will handle all manuscripts from their initial submission; they assign reviewers, and they make decisions (reject, revise, conditionally accept) and communicate those decisions to the authors. While Special Issues are always accompanied by an Open Call for Papers, Guest Editors are also encouraged to reach out to potential contributors to solicit quality submissions. All manuscripts for the Special Issue must undergo double-blind peer review and revisions according to normal SER review process and in accordance with SER’s editorial policy and formal guidelines. Final acceptance of papers is done in consultation with the Chief Editors of SER.

A special issue typically has 6-10 regular length papers plus editors’ introduction. SER manuscripts are generally no longer than 10,000 words in length (inclusive of references, but excluding tables, figures, appendices and online appendices). Manuscripts should follow a clear line of argument and be written in a concise style without sacrificing meaningful content.

Proposals and queries may be sent to chief editors Akos Rona-Tas and Alya Guseva.

Application Deadline: 30 September 2026

[Call for Papers] Call for sessions: World Economic History Congress 2028 (Montevideo, July 2028) https://www.heterodoxnews.com/n/htn363.html#art-17592186132152 https://www.heterodoxnews.com/n/htn363.html#art-17592186132152#363 Call for Papers Mon, 24 Aug 2026 00:00:00 +0000

Deadline: 14 September 2026

24-28 July, 2028 | Montevideo, Uruguay

Conference theme: World Powers and Conflicts

The 21st World Economic History Congress will convene from 24 to 28 July 2028 in Montevideo, Uruguay. The IEHA has a particular interest in strengthening the scientific approach to the historical and social sciences and in promoting exchange, cooperation, and understanding among all people.

The theme of the Congress is World Powers and Conflicts, which highlights central issues facing humanity today and connects to a broad and diverse range of historical problems, particularly those concerned with resources, inequality, and sustainability, central topics of the last two congresses (Paris and Lund).

Sessions may be proposed by any member of the international economic history community, whatever their institutional affiliation or status, as well as by scholars in related disciplines. The organizers strongly encourage proposals from early-career researchers. Sessions can also be proposed by non-national IEHA member organizations.

Submissions are welcome on the economic and social histories of all places and periods, and the organizers especially encourage proposals from the global South. Given the diversity of the membership, the organizers will consider any submission that advances the study, teaching, and public presentation of economic history. The organizers welcome panel proposals that highlight emerging scholarship from different fields of economic history, as well as contributions on innovative methodological and theoretical approaches.

The 5-day Montevideo Congress will feature approximately 180 sessions, with each day divided into 90-minute blocks (two before and two after lunch). It will be possible to combine two sessions into larger, coherent units. The proposals must make clear whether they apply to one or two blocks.

Please find more info here.

Submission Deadline: 14 September 2026

24-26 May, 2027 | Vienna, Austria

Conference theme: Democracy Under Pressure: Conditions of the Authoritarian Turn Yesterday and Today

The conference brings together scholars from law and socioeconomics to examine the current rise of authoritarian tendencies around the world and to explore which socioeconomic, legal, and institutional responses could strengthen democratic resilience. The conference addresses these challenges in dialogue with four pivotal thinkers – Friedrich Hayek, Karl Polanyi, Hans Kelsen, and Carl Schmitt – whose influential yet antagonistic accounts of the proper economic and constitutional order remain highly relevant for contemporary debate. Confirmed keynote speakers are Katharina Pistor (Columbia University) and Quinn Slobodian (Boston University).

The organizers welcome the submission of individual abstracts as well as proposals for complete panels from scholars in law, socioeconomics, political economy, constitutional theory, political science, economic sociology, history and related research fields — at all career stages, and from all regions, including the Global South.

[Call for Papers] Joint CEPR-UCD-Central Bank of Ireland workshop (Dublin, November 2026) https://www.heterodoxnews.com/n/htn363.html#art-17592186132206 https://www.heterodoxnews.com/n/htn363.html#art-17592186132206#363 Call for Papers Mon, 24 Aug 2026 00:00:00 +0000

Deadline: 28 August 2026

13 November, 2026 | Dublin, Ireland

Workshop theme: The Return of Industrial Policy: Historical Lessons and Contemporary Challenges

Industrial policy has returned to the centre stage of economic policymaking. Across the EU, the US, and East Asia, governments are increasingly intervening to support strategic sectors, strengthen supply chains, accelerate the green transition, and secure technological leadership. Initiatives such as the EU Green Deal Industrial Plan, the Net-Zero Industry Act, and the European and US Chips Acts reflect a broader shift toward active state involvement in industrial transformation and economic security. After decades in which industrial policy played a more limited role in advanced economies, geopolitical tensions, supply-chain disruptions, and decarbonisation have renewed interest in state-led economic coordination. Consequently, questions surrounding subsidies, strategic protection, industrial targeting, innovation policy, and economic resilience have returned to the forefront of academic research and policymaking.

While of contemporary relevance, government efforts to shape industrial development have a long history. States have long sought to influence the direction and location of economic activity. This historical record provides a valuable laboratory for understanding past successes and failures and informing future policy.

The organizers invite completed papers or extended abstracts by Friday 28 August 2026, with preference given to completed papers. Applications are welcome from researchers at all career stages. Submissions will be selected on originality, analytical rigor, and policy relevance.

The workshop will feature a keynote lecture by Prof. Claudia Steinwender (LMU Munich & CEPR) and a panel discussion on the future of industrial policy in Ireland.

Please email your paper or extended abstract (PDF) to info.indpolhistory@gmail.com.

Submission Deadline: 28 August 2026

[Call for Papers] Journal of Institutional Economics: Symposium on "The Institutional Foundations of Stakeholder Theory. Insights from Original and Non-Mainstream Institutional Economics" https://www.heterodoxnews.com/n/htn363.html#art-17592186132129 https://www.heterodoxnews.com/n/htn363.html#art-17592186132129#363 Call for Papers Mon, 24 Aug 2026 00:00:00 +0000

Deadline: 31 January 2027

Stakeholder theory is often presented as an ethical correction to shareholder primacy. That framing captures an important normative disagreement, but it leaves the theory’s institutional content underdeveloped. Firms and corporations are not neutral containers within which managers decide whose interests to consider. They are institutional arrangements constituted by formal and informal rules that allocate authority, voice, property claims, responsibilities, exposure to risk, and access to remedies.

The stakeholder question is therefore not only whether managers should care about non-shareholding groups. It is how institutions define relevant participants, organise their interdependence, structure conflicts, distribute decision rights, and adapt when existing rules cease to support viable cooperation.

The symposium’s organising question

How do institutions constitute stakeholder relationships, distribute authority and vulnerability among stakeholder groups, and evolve in response to conflict, uncertainty, power, and changing social and ecological conditions?

Original institutional economics offers powerful resources for this task. Veblen directs attention to evolving habits, technologies, power structures, and ceremonial valuations. Commons treats institutions as collective action that controls, liberates, and expands individual action, and analyses transactions as legally and socially constituted relations involving conflict, dependence, bargaining, and working rules. Later institutionalist work extends these insights through social provisioning, cumulative causation, institutional change, and the legal-economic nexus.

The symposium also welcomes contributions drawing on post-Keynesian, feminist, ecological, behavioural, humanistic, evolutionary, social, legal, comparative, polycentric, and organisational approaches. These traditions are relevant when they illuminate the design, operation, persistence, change, or comparative effects of identifiable institutions. The collection will not be a loose set of critiques of mainstream economics; it will be a focused institutional analysis of stakeholder governance.

Please find more info here.

Submission Deadline: 31 January 2027

[Call for Papers] MARXISM21: Special Issue on "Marxian Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence" https://www.heterodoxnews.com/n/htn363.html#art-17592186131899 https://www.heterodoxnews.com/n/htn363.html#art-17592186131899#363 Call for Papers Mon, 24 Aug 2026 00:00:00 +0000

Deadline: 31 December 2026

MARXISM21, founded in 2004, is a bi-lingual (Korean and English), quarterly academic journal specialized in Marxist studies. The editors are planning the special issue on ‘Marxian Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence’ for the Autumn 2027 (to be published on August 20, 2027).

The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence and large-scale machine learning systems across economy and everyday life demands engagement from the Marxist tradition. AI raises questions about the core categories Marxism uses to analyze capitalism such as labor, value, class, and ownership of the means of production, etc. Marx's own writing on machinery and the general intellect in Grundrisse, along with later Marxist work on automation and technological unemployment, provides a foundation on which this discussion builds. This special issue invites theoretical, empirical, and historical contributions that interrogate AI through Marxian theory.

  • Topics of interest include, but are not limited to:
  • The relevance of labor theory of value in a AI-driven economy
  • How do AI and automation affect technological progress and the tendency of the rate of profit to fall
  • Are data new factor of production?
  • AI-driven labor process transformations and the real subsumption of labor
  • Technofeudalism-related topics, etc.

Those interested in contributing to this special issue are kindly requested to send a tentative title and a short abstract to Dong-Min Rieu by December 31, 2026. The deadline for submitting final manuscripts (max. 12,000 words length) is May 31, 2027.

Submission Deadline: 31 December 2026

[Call for Participants] Macroeconomic Transformation Hub: Rethinking Macroeconomic Planning in Europe (Berlin, October 2026) https://www.heterodoxnews.com/n/htn363.html#art-17592186132008 https://www.heterodoxnews.com/n/htn363.html#art-17592186132008#363 Call for Participants Mon, 24 Aug 2026 00:00:00 +0000


October 15, 2026, 09:00 – 12:00 CET | Auditorium at the Jacob-und-Wilhelm-Grimm-Zentrum, Geschwister-Scholl-Straße 1–3, 10117 Berlin (Raum E’701)

Organized by the Network for Pluralist Economics in cooperation with the research project “Heterodox Planning” (Humboldt University/Einstein Foundation)

Europe stands at a critical macroeconomic crossroads. As the continent grapples with the compounding pressures of structural economic crisis, geopolitical fragmentation, and the urgent need for unprecedented socio-ecological investment, conventional market-driven paradigms are failing to provide viable answers.

As highlighted in the recent landscape report by Partners for a New Economy (P4NE), “Fertile Ground: Exploring Europe’s New Economy Ecosystem”, if we are to successfully navigate this era of interlocking crises, the field must elevate macroeconomic planning. No longer dismissed as a relic of the past, strategic public coordination and structural steering are re-emerging as essential tools to reshape the future of European capital, navigate fiscal rules, and steer the green transition. This event brings together leading voices in political economy to dissect how democratic, structural economic planning can be effectively revived and translated to viable policy solutions.

The Panel

Ilias Alami (Assistant Professor at the University of Cambridge, Member of the Green Planning Comission) – will illustrate how the global rise of state-owned enterprises and sovereign wealth funds expands the scope for progressive economic intervention, while questioning how we can push past these frameworks toward deeper systemic transformation.

Jacob Hasselbalch (Associate Professor at Copenhagen Business School) will compare historical and contemporary planning models—spanning France, Denmark, South Korea, and China—to show how states can deploy long-term macroeconomic steering, indicative planning, and strategic investment budgets to manage the green transition.

Hannah Bensussan (Political Economist and EU Economic Policy Expert; Advanced background in institutional economics) will analyze the current French institutional landscape, critique the successes and failures of its planning ministry, and explore how the macroeconomic proposals of La France Insoumise can be expanded for broader European policy.

Moderated by Maxine Fowé (Political Economist and journalist)

Agenda

  • 09:00 – Welcome & Opening Remarks by the Network for Pluralist Economics
  • 09:15 – Flash Talks on Macroeconomic Planning
  • 10:15 – Open Q&A Session
  • 11:30 – Networking & Refreshments (until 12:30)

After the MacroHub workshop: Age of Planning Conference

The exploration of macroeconomic planning continues in the rest of the day and on October 16 with the academic conference “Age of Planning”, which brings together empirical research on corporate and state planning in practice. More information will be sent after registration for the MacroHub.

Register for the MacroHub here.

[Conference Papers, Reports, and Podcasts] ASE Member Spotlight: Jon Wisman https://www.heterodoxnews.com/n/htn363.html#art-17592186132191 https://www.heterodoxnews.com/n/htn363.html#art-17592186132191#363 Conference Papers, Reports, and Podcasts Mon, 24 Aug 2026 00:00:00 +0000

In this interview, Professor Jon Wisman discusses his book, Why We Must Work: Economic Freedom, Fulfilling Work, and Workplace Democracy. Wisman outlines the central premise of his work: human beings evolved to find work naturally fulfilling, pleasurable, and integrated with leisure, community, and social respect. However, the rise of elite-controlled states roughly 5,500 years ago debased work into an unpleasant means of survival under external command—a view perpetuated by mainstream economics, which treats work as “disutility”.

Wisman argues that despite reaching material abundance in rich nations, modern society faces widespread insecurity, stress, and dissatisfaction because it prioritizes consumption over fulfilling work. To restore work to a source of human thriving, he proposes two major structural reforms within a market framework: guaranteed employment (a job guarantee) and workplace democracy (worker ownership and democratic control). He emphasizes that an interdisciplinary approach—incorporating anthropology, history, and psychology—is essential to understanding these economic dynamics. Ultimately, he frames workplace democracy and reduced inequality not only as economic improvements, but as urgent political necessities to preserve democracy and avoid global ecological collapse.

[Conference Papers, Reports, and Podcasts] ASE Member Spotlight: Muzna Alvi https://www.heterodoxnews.com/n/htn363.html#art-17592186132115 https://www.heterodoxnews.com/n/htn363.html#art-17592186132115#363 Conference Papers, Reports, and Podcasts Mon, 24 Aug 2026 00:00:00 +0000

In this interview, Salewa Olewoye spoke with Dr. Muzna Alvi, a Research Fellow at the International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI) and the winner of the prestigious ASE Helen Potter Award. The conversation centers on Dr. Alvi’s award-winning research examining the complex dynamics of gender, caste, religion, and female labor force participation in India.

Key Takeaways from the Discussion

  • India’s Unique Paradox: Unlike typical economic development trends, India experienced a multi-decade decline in female labor force participation. Dr. Alvi breaks down the factors behind this shift, including changing cultural norms, structural shifts in a services-led economy, longer schooling for young women, and data measurement biases.
  • The Intersection of Religion and Caste: The interview explores why communities with similar economic deprivations exhibit vastly different labor outcomes. Dr. Alvi addresses why Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribe (SC/ST) women display high rates of labor participation while Muslim women face significantly lower rates, attributing much of this disparity to economic “ghettoization” and local job availability rather than purely cultural factors.
  • Policy Approaches & Solutions: Dr. Alvi highlights practical pathways forward, emphasizing the role of India’s self-help group movement, national workfare programs, and the vital necessity of supporting smallholder agriculture where most rural women are employed.

[Job Postings] Leuphana University, Germany https://www.heterodoxnews.com/n/htn363.html#art-17592186132148 https://www.heterodoxnews.com/n/htn363.html#art-17592186132148#363 Job Postings Mon, 24 Aug 2026 00:00:00 +0000

Deadline: 9 September 2026

Full professorship „Economics and Security“ (W3)

The Leuphana Centre for Cooperative Security (LCCS) is seeking a distinguished researcher to join. The professorship represents the area Economics and Security in research and teaching. The professorship is based at the Institute of Economics and contributes to the establishment and leadership of the LCCS.

The Leuphana Centre for Cooperative Security (LCCS) is an interdisciplinary center for research on security that combines the subjects of law, economics, political science, and psychology. Premised on a broad conception of security that goes beyond the traditional focus on the military security of states, it conducts basic research on the conditions under which cooperation may enhance or undermine security in three principal areas: international security, internal security and economic security. The LCCS also develops recommendations for action in politics, business, and society, focusing on cooperative solutions to the consequences of diverse security threats for Germany in the European context. As a space for research and debate on the pressing security issues of the 21st century, the LCCS connects researchers from Leuphana, Germany, and around the world with expert representatives from the field. The position strengthens the Institute of Economics and the School of Public Affairs by advancing their shared focus on “evidence-based policy” and “resilient society” within the University‘s “Embracing Transformation” framework.

For this position, the LCCS is seeking an outstanding researcher with an international profile to contribute to research on economic security, with a focus on macroeconomics at the intersection of international economic relations and defense economics generating a lasting impact in their field as well as for society. The research areas include topics such as (de-)globalization and international economic (dis)integration, economic dependencies and the resilience of international trade relations and supply chains. Further relevant topics are international financial integration, public finance, as well as the protection of key economic sectors and geoeconomic analyses related to international trade policy, multinational investment, and economic sanctions.

Recruitment and Communications Coordinator

The Levy Economics Institute of Bard College, an internationally recognized policy research organization, invites applications for the position of Recruitment and Communications Coordinator. The Recruitment and Communications Coordinator will primarily be responsible for graduate recruitment and publicizing the Institute’s research activities and its innovative Master’s in Economic Theory and Policy degree programs.

Responsibilities:

  • Working with the Director of Graduate Programs on admissions strategy and outreach, including maintaining the Graduate Program web presence, arranging for applicant webinars, mailings, and recruiting schedules of the graduate program
  • The ideal candidate is motivated and charismatic, with great communication skills and the ability to cultivate applications and plan well in advance of key recruiting milestones and deadlines
  • The Coordinator is the primary contact for all incoming students and must be responsive to student requests and questions
  • Acting as the primary contact for graduate-program-related campus offices (student accounts, financial aid, international student services, etc.)
  • Traveling to regional colleges and graduate school fairs, especially during the fall recruiting season
  • Actively publicizing the Institute’s research and events through social media and an e-newsletter, including preparing synopses of new publications
  • Posting to and managing content on the Institute webpage

Qualifications:

  • The institute is seeking an individual who possesses excellent writing skills, has the ability to operate across multiple issue areas in economic theory and public policy, and can package these research ideas appropriately and communicate them clearly to a broad range of audiences. A degree in economics/public policy or experience as an economics/public policy writer are preferred. Familiarity with (or a willingness to learn) the Adobe suite (including Adobe Express for graphics) is a plus.
  • An ability to energetically articulate the Levy Graduate Program. The successful candidate must be able to speak in front of groups of potential graduate students and communicate effectively and collaboratively with various staff and faculty associated with the graduate programs, including relevant Bard College staff.
  • Previous higher education experience is valued, as is experience with admission and application software (e.g., Slate), but a willingness to learn and manage such programs is essential.
  • A bachelor’s degree (preferably in economics or a related field) is required.

To Apply:

Please provide a cover letter, resume, writing sample, and the contact information for three professional references to Interfolio by following this link.

Deadline: 28 August 2026

PhD position - '(Dis)orderly transitions: The financial sector's role in shaping just energy transitions'

What the project is about

In recent years the idea of an 'orderly just transition' has started to gain ground. While questions of justice have been taken up by ‘just transition’ research, the addition of 'orderly' is more recent, raising new questions around the envisioned speed, direction, and outcomes of energy transitions. In this project we want to look at this idea of 'order' in transitions more closely, identifying and analysing how (some) actors in the financial sector try to implement an orderly transition away from fossil fuels through the use of specific financial instruments and practices. By incorporating ideas from both political economy and economic sociology the project investigates how attempts at enacting order by financial actors can be understood as a process of contested temporal politics, with actors seeking to make the future knowable, trajectories towards it manageable, and outcomes controllable.

Who you will be working with

The project is a collaboration between myself (Bregje van Veelen, Lund University) and Amy Janzwood at McGill University in Canada, and will include cases in both North America and Scandinavia. The PhD candidate in Lund is expected to focus primarily on the latter, but there will be opportunity for comparative work too. The position is based at LUCSUS (Lund University Centre for Sustainability Studies) in Sweden, where you will be part of a friendly and supportive community of scholars.

What the institution is looking for in a candidate

Someone with a strong interest in critical social science approaches who is excited to explore how issues of politics and power play out in the financial sphere. The project speaks to a variety of themes and concepts, including energy transitions, sustainable finance, temporalities & future-making, and social constructions of risk. The institution does not expect anyone to be experienced with all of these, but having experience with one of these topics and an interest in some of the others is important. Most of the data collection is expected to be qualitative in nature, so experience with qualitative methods is a must. Knowledge of a Scandinavian language is a bonus, but not a requirement.

For potential applicants unfamiliar with the Swedish system

PhD positions in Sweden are fully funded for 4 years. You'll receive a regular salary, vacation days, pension contributions, etc. In addition to conducting research, you will be expected to complete 60 credits (=one year) of course work. There are also opportunities for teaching, and taking on administrative/leadership roles (such as PhD rep), for which you will receive extra time (and funding) to complete your PhD.

More details on the position and how to apply here.

Application Deadline: 28 August 2026

Deadline: 10 September 2026

Assistant Professor in International Relations and International Political Economy

The Department of Political Science at the University of Amsterdam invites applications for a tenure-track Assistant Professor (‘Universitair Docent’) position in Political Science. Based in the Political Economy and Transnational Governance (PETGOV) programme group, the department welcomes new members whose research (and teaching) is informed by and connected to ongoing global transformations. The ideal candidate brings an innovative research agenda, experience, and enthusiasm to complement our programme group's research and to educate our students.

For this Assistant Professor vacancy, the department seeks to strengthen its expertise on inter-state relations (diplomacy, inter-state conflict and alliances, global security) in the context of geo-political economy and combined with a rigorous methodological approach. For this position the department particularly seeks candidates who approach such questions empirically from a global perspective rather than only from a specific regional angle.  

Candidates for the position should complement PETGOV’s research community, a group interested in not just national or inter-national political relations but also non-nation-state global economic and political relations. Finally, candidates should be ready to contribute to the teaching of core courses in International Relations and/or political economy.

Core tasks

  • Teaching general and specialist courses in international relations / (International) Political Economy at both undergraduate and post-graduate levels, and involvement in post-graduate supervision;
  • Developing, conducting, and supervising high quality academic research on topics mentioned above;
  • Participating in acquiring external research funding;
  • Contributing to the research programme of the Programme Group PETGOV and the Amsterdam Institute for Social Science Research through scholarly publications and engagement in local, national, and international networks.

What do you have to offer

  • A completed and submitted doctoral thesis in Political Science – specifically in international relations / political economy, or a closely related field;
  • An innovative research programme and output that demonstrates excellence and provides potential for raising external research funding;
  • Research added value (future ambitions, and ideas about how these match or fill niches within the programme group);
  • Mastery of up-to-date research methods appropriate for your research agenda;
  • Substantial academic teaching experience – at both undergraduate and postgraduate levels– on a breadth of topics within the discipline / scope of the profile and on a variety of teaching formats such as lectures, seminars, and supervision, including (partially) independently designed courses.
  • Broad academic teaching orientation, able and willing to teach general international relations, and/or political economy courses.
  • Well-developed teaching and didactic vision showing demonstrated capacity to inspire and activate students, encourage in-class interaction, address contemporary, sensitive or topical issues, and foster bridges between academia and society.
  • The ability to work both as an independent professional and as a team player, with an appreciation for diversity and inclusion, reflected in a proven track record of good academic citizenship;
  • The ability to develop connections to practitioners/policymakers/stakeholders to the benefit of teaching and research;
  • The proven ability to develop and submit competitive research grant proposals; 
  • A capacity to teach in English and Dutch (or a willingness to acquire knowledge of Dutch within three years);
  • The basic qualification at Dutch universities in higher education (‘Basiskwalificatie Onderwijs’; BKO) certificate, or a willingness to acquire such.

If you recognize yourself in the profile and are interested in either role, the department looks forward to receiving your motivation letter outlining your potential contribution to the education and research programmes mentioned above. Please also submit your CV, including (i) past work experience and qualifications (research, teaching, and/or management), (ii) your research interest(s), and (iii) a list of publications. In addition, the department also wants to ask you for a single-page teaching statement explaining your teaching experience, ambition and vision. Make sure that your application states to which of position you are applying. As there are multiple vacancies open for the Department of Political Science and PETGOV, know that there is no obstacle or disadvantage to applying for multiple positions.

Deadline: 21 August 2026

Postdoctoral position for a researcher in social sciences (3 years full-time, compliant with international mobility condition)

The Centre for Public and Social Law is recruiting a postdoctoral fellow to join our team based at the Université Libre de Bruxelles (ULB) in Brussels. The fellow will contribute to the research project entitled 'Rethinking work beyond productivism from labour law and its uses' (RethinkingWork).

This research is funded by an ERC Starting Grant awarded to Elise Dermine, professor at the Université Libre de Bruxelles and financed between 2025 and 2030. In the context of the green transition, the project aims to develop concrete trajectories and public policies to emancipate work from productivism, and to better support activities with eco-social value. The proposed trajectories will be based on a European and comparative study of labour law and its social uses.

The successful candidate will be tasked with developing a typology of the post-productivist dimension of national labour law systems, drawing on clustering methods and the results of the European comparative survey. In collaboration with Elise Dermine, he or she will also carry out a foresight exercise that will aim to identify the risks and opportunities associated with potential trajectories through participatory workshops with European stakeholders (including DG EMPL, European social partners and European environmental movements). He or she will also support and/or lead on the following activities: organising national and international conferences and seminars, writing scientific articles, coordinating a special issue or book, and carrying out administrative tasks related to the research project.

Required qualifications and criteria:

  • You hold a PhD in social sciences or can demonstrate that you will hold it by the end of September 2026.
  • You will have been holding your PhD for a maximum of 8 years by 1 September 2026.
  • You have not been living or carrying out your main activity (employment, studies, etc.) in Belgium for more than 24 months during the 3 years immediately preceding 1 September 2026 (international mobility condition).
  • You have an excellent knowledge of written and spoken English.

Desirable skills and professional experience:

  • You have experience in comparative social policies and skills in clustering methods.
  • If you have experience in foresight methodologies, this is an advantage.
  • If you have experience in collaborating with stakeholders at the EU level (DG EMPL, European social partners and/or European environmental movements), this is an advantage.
  • You enjoy working in a team and have experience of successfully managing several projects at once.
  • You have excellent written and verbal communication skills.

If you have further questions, please contact Elise Dermine.
